A person's recovery codes are issued with their first one and act as a second factor once each. | Belongs to one E3; a person has 0..n. | A passkey counts only with user verification (fingerprint, face or PIN). Added, replaced or removed only as R54 allows. | active, removed |

| E26 | **Fleet central** | The one Fleet service of the deployment. | Holds 0..n E1, each in its own storage, with that organization's E2, E6 enrollments, E7, E15, E21 and E24. Reached only through the sign-in service. | Not reachable from the internet. Holds no organization's state in another's storage, and refuses any request whose organization differs from the storage it reaches (R55). | — |

| R34 | Every workspace and fleet machine MUST belong to exactly one organization. A session belongs to its machine's organization, and its project MUST be in that organization. A person MAY be a member of several. No machine allowance, session registration, remote start, message or token MAY span two organizations; a request that would MUST be refused with nothing changed and nothing about the other organization revealed. **Until step 3**, a machine still reads every workspace of its own organization (see [Requirements: what stays as today](requirements.html#requirements--after-the-switch)); it never reads another organization's. | E1, E2, E6, E7, E15 | U27, P6, O6 |

| R55 | Fleet central (E26) MUST NOT be reachable from the internet: every request MUST reach it only through the sign-in service, over a link that only the sign-in service holds. Each organization's state MUST be held in that organization's own storage, apart from every other organization's, and central MUST refuse, with nothing changed, any request whose organization differs from the storage it reaches. Creating an organization MUST NOT need a deployment. A Router MUST be given only the sign-in address and the organization. | E1, E6, E26 | U45, U27, U15 |

| R13 | Only a person whose role holds the permission (E27, U46) MAY: invite people to an organization or remove them (`member`); create workspaces; allow or withdraw a machine's allowance; approve or deny a device-code login; revoke a machine's enrollment; remove a session; set the token lifetime; and read the lookups (R14) and the who-is-logged-in view (R49).
In this design only the owner holds any permission, so "the admin" below means the owner. Only the deployment's configured owner MAY create an organization (A5, 3 November), and the creator becomes the new organization's owner. In this design an organization has one owner, its creator, who can't be removed or demoted; handing over comes later and MUST keep at least one owner. There is no fleet-wide role: the roles are owner and member, with managers to come (OD24, U46). Open sign-up, where anyone signed in may create an organization, waits with the people sign-in design's SD2.
The permission is checked live by the sign-in service, for the organization the action belongs to, with the person signed in to that organization and current there, at the time of the action as the people sign-in design's R9, R19 and R20 require (its freshness bound SD8); the confirmation it attaches names the permission it checked (OD25). Each change also needs R53's second factor. Creating a workspace is one step at Fleet central (4 November, B2), so it's checked and applied together, with no later application.
Each admin change MUST be recorded, as the people sign-in design's R12 requires. A change Fleet central applies is recorded in the same step as the change; a change whose record can't be written MUST NOT happen. A people change the sign-in service applies (inviting, removing) MUST be recorded before it happens, and refused if the record can't be written; its outcome is recorded after, and a record whose outcome was never written stays unconfirmed (OD26).
Anyone else MUST be refused with nothing changed and nothing revealed: a member, another organization's owner, a person no longer a member, a session no longer current, a bot or a session. | E1, E2, E6, E7, E15, E19, E21, E23 | U21, U20, U31 |

| R14 | For a person, the system MUST answer their membership in the organization asked about (a member with a role, invited, or not a member), from the sign-in service, never another organization (R34). For a session: its machine, project, workspace and isolation record. For a workspace: the machines allowed to serve it. For a machine: its organization, its enrollment's state and what authorized it, its allowed workspaces, and its shared bucket. | E1, E3, E6, E7, E13, E14, E15, E21 | U9, O3 |

| R27 | Every request from the sign-in service to Fleet central (C7) MUST arrive over the link that only the sign-in service holds (R55), and MUST be for an operation C7 names. From the internet, the sign-in service MUST pass on only machine connections and people's admin requests. A machine connection carries no person confirmation and needs none (R40). To each person's request it MUST attach its own confirmation that the person's session is current and that their role there holds the permission the request needs (E27), discarding any a caller sent. It MUST send the decisions (device-login, machine-token and organization-provisioning) only on its own behalf, from facts it verified itself, never as a request passed on from the internet. A request for another operation, or one naming an organization the person or machine it acts for may not act in, MUST be refused and change nothing. Repeating an accepted request MUST have no further effect beyond what C7 states. Central's only request to the sign-in service MUST be reading its published signing keys; central MUST send it nothing that asks, decides or changes anything. | all | U15, U16 |

| R53 | **Step-up.** Each change R13 reserves for the admin MUST be refused with nothing changed unless the admin's sign-in includes a second factor (E25) confirmed no more than 15 minutes (one setting) before the change. Those changes are: inviting or removing a person, changing a person's role, creating a workspace, changing a machine's allowances, approving or denying a device-code login, revoking an enrollment, removing a session and setting the token lifetime. The refusal MUST say that a second factor is needed.
One exception: approving a device-code login into an organization that has never had an enrollment MAY rely on the provider sign-in alone.
A second factor confirms on top of the same person's provider sign-in. A passkey sign-in with user verification counts as both factors, so its new session is confirmed from that moment (OD21); a passkey assertion without user verification MUST NOT sign in or confirm anything.
Reading (the lookups and the who-is-logged-in view) needs no second factor. A passkey confirms only with user verification. | E1, E3, E21, E25 | U43, U21 |

| R51 | **Telemetry.** Fleet central, the sign-in service and the Router MUST each leave one structured record for every decision and every refusal on the login, connection, registration, presence, activity, remote-start and view paths, and for each outbox step. A record MUST name its kind, its outcome with a bounded reason class, and the identifiers involved (organization, enrollment, installation, connection, session, client), and nothing else from the request.
No record, trace attribute or span name MAY contain a token, refresh credential, device code, user code, client secret, cookie, authorization header, private key or email address.
On Cloudflare, both Workers MUST turn on Workers Logs, Fleet central MUST also turn on Workers traces, and each MUST export what it keeps over OTLP to the destinations the deployment names (OD17). The sign-in Worker's automatic traces and invocation logs MUST stay off, because they record each request's full URL, and OAuth callbacks carry the provider's one-time code in theirs. Fleet central MAY keep its automatic records because nothing it receives carries a secret in its URL (machine, service and Access credentials travel in headers), but none of them MAY contain the value of a credential-bearing header (`Authorization`, cookies, Cloudflare Access credentials). A secret a caller deliberately places in a URL to central is outside this guarantee. On Node and Tokio, the same records MUST be exported over OTLP to the endpoint the deployment configures, and with none configured they are written to the host's own output only. Each service MUST leave the same records on each of its hosts.
A telemetry failure (a destination down, missing or slow) MUST NOT change or delay any answer. | all | U41, U16 |

| R29 | All the sign-in service's persistent state MUST be in SQLite through Drizzle: D1 through Drizzle on Cloudflare, a `better-sqlite3` file through Drizzle on Node. Better Auth MUST reach it through its Drizzle adapter. Its schema MUST change only through migrations `drizzle-kit` generates and the repository checks in, and each database MUST apply them through exactly one mechanism before it serves a request.
No Kysely or `node:sqlite` MAY appear in its code or tests, and no code MAY execute SQL text. Queries use the Drizzle query builder, which MAY include its `sql` template for an expression inside a builder call with bound parameters, but never `sql.raw(`, `db.run\|all\|get\|values(sql…)`, or a driver's own `.prepare(` or `.exec(`.
**Your gate (OD4):** you approve the schema and its migrations before code uses them. | E3, E23 | U22 |

| R30 | Every sign-in rule (the token-kind dispatch, the final checks before a token is released, the permission check, the device-code approval, the service-request receivers, the audit, the who-is-logged-in page) MUST live in one runtime-free core. The core MUST reach storage, time, identifiers, cryptography and outbound requests only through capabilities its host supplies, and each capability is required. The Cloudflare host and the Node host MUST each supply them and add no sign-in rule. As with Fleet central's core crate and its Tokio and Cloudflare hosts, the core MUST be its own package that depends on neither runtime: no Cloudflare or Node types and no SQLite driver. Each host MUST be its own package that depends on the core, never the reverse. | E3, E23 | U23, U16 |

| R31 | Each decision that writes more than one row MUST hold without an interactive transaction, because D1 has none: it MUST be either one conditional statement, or a fixed batch whose later statements stay correct when an earlier conditional statement changes no row. A decision MUST NOT read a row in code and then write on the strength of that read. In particular:
- an unknown answer from central MUST NOT be treated as a refusal;
- a device code MUST be consumed at most once, however many concurrent polls redeem it. | E3, E23 | U22, U16, U33 |

| R32 | No UUID other than version 7 MAY be minted or stored by the sign-in service. Every identifier it mints as a UUID, and every model identifier Better Auth gets from its configured generator, MUST be a UUIDv7.
Two kinds of value aren't UUIDs and keep their own form. Secret material (client secrets, session tokens, PKCE verifiers, signing keys, device codes and user codes) MUST stay random secret bytes or codes. A key Better Auth derives from presented data to make something single-use (the client-assertion record keyed by a digest of the assertion's `jti`) MUST stay derived, because a fresh identifier would remove the replay protection. | E3, E23 | U24 |

| R33 | No sign-in test, test helper or test harness MAY read the real clock or wait on real time. Tests wait only on events (a process's exit, a readiness message, a returned promise), and every timer runs on a controlled clock or mocked timers. Time-dependent behavior, including the expiries Better Auth computes itself, MUST be exercised with a controlled clock, and no production build MAY be changed to make that possible. The tests MUST include Hegel property tests of at least: the token-kind dispatch over every client kind, grant and resource; the device code's single use under concurrent redemption; and the token claims' parse round trip. | E22, E23 | U25 |

| V9 | R13, C4 | Your admin actions apply with their records: inviting and removing a person, creating a workspace, allowing a machine, approving a device code, revoking an enrollment. A member (whose role holds no permission), another organization's owner, a removed member, a stale session, a bot and a session are each refused with nothing changed and nothing revealed; so is a request whose attached confirmation names a different permission, organization or person than the request. Only an organization's owner creates an organization, and the creator owns it; a member can't. The last owner can't be removed. A change central applies whose record can't be written doesn't happen; people changes are recorded first and refused if the record can't be written (OD26). | An unauthorized action applies, reveals something, a confirmation for one permission authorizes another, or a change applies without its record. |

| V19 | R27, C7 | Each C7 operation sent by the sign-in service over its link is accepted. A request reaching central any other way is refused or finds no route. An operation C7 doesn't name, a body naming an organization the person or machine it acts for may not act in, a body whose organization differs from the storage it reaches, and a malformed body are each refused with nothing changed. A repeat has only the effect C7 states. Central sends the sign-in service nothing beyond reading its published keys; after a revoke, the sign-in service disables that machine's client. (The machine token's clock edges, including `grant_expires_at`, belong to V32.) | Central answers a request that didn't come over the link, accepts another operation or an out-of-scope organization, asks the sign-in service anything beyond its published keys, or a repeat changes more than C7 allows. |

| V21 | R29 | The sign-in service runs on D1 and on a `better-sqlite3` file through Drizzle and Better Auth's Drizzle adapter. A database built from the checked-in migrations serves every case. A scan finds no Kysely, `node:sqlite`, `sql.raw(`, `db.run\|all\|get\|values(sql`, or a driver's own `.prepare(` or `.exec(`. Your approval (OD4) is recorded before the first commit using the schema. | SQL text runs outside the query builder, Kysely remains, a database serves before its migrations run, or code that uses the schema predates your approval. |

| V22 | R30 | The same sign-in suite passes on the Cloudflare host and the Node host, and a core run with recording capabilities shows every time, identifier, crypto and outbound use went through them. | A rule lives in one host, or the core reaches a platform global. |

| V23 | R31 | Each multi-row decision gives the same result on D1 and `better-sqlite3`, and an unknown answer from central is never treated as a refusal. Concurrent redemptions of one approved device code yield exactly one machine login. | An unknown answer is treated as a refusal, a decision holds on one database only, or a device code logs in twice. |

| V24 | R32 | Every UUID-shaped identifier stored during the sign-in suite is version 7. Client-assertion records carry the derived `jti` digest key, and a replayed assertion is refused. No secret, device code or user code is a UUID. | A version-4 or version-5 UUID anywhere; a client-assertion record with a fresh random key; a UUID used as a secret or code. |

| V25 | R33 | A scan of the sign-in tests, their helpers and their harness finds no real-clock read, no real-time wait, and no real timer: no hang-guard timeout and no wall-clock log timestamp. Every wait is on an event. Expiries are crossed by moving a controlled clock; the four Hegel families exist and run. | A test depends on real time, or an expiry is only tested by waiting. |

| V26 | R34 | An allowance, registration, remote start, message or token that would span two organizations is each refused with nothing changed and nothing revealed. | V43 | R51 | After a login, a refusal, a connection, a registration and a view refresh, the OTLP collector holds one record for each, naming its kind, outcome and identifiers. A harmless canary placed in the sign-in Worker's request URLs appears in no record Cloudflare keeps, and no credential carried in a header appears in any record Cloudflare keeps for central. | A decision leaves no record, a record carries a secret, the two hosts of one service leave different records, a stopped collector changes an answer, a sign-in URL's contents reach a record Cloudflare keeps, or a header credential reaches one of central's. |

A passkey sign-in with user verification is confirmed from the start; one without it signs in nothing and confirms nothing. | A change goes through on Google alone, the window isn't enforced, the first-machine exception covers a second machine, or reads demand a second factor. |

A machine already logged in to org A is refused an approval into org B, with nothing written in either. A new organization created by an owner works at once, with no deploy. A Router given only the sign-in address and the organization logs in and connects. | Central answers a request that didn't come through the sign-in service, one organization's data lands in another's storage, a machine is in two organizations, a new organization needs a deploy, or a Router needs anything else typed in. |

b2-data-text.text:
Two new tables, both in each organization's Fleet store, following your table rule: a UUIDv7 key, `created_at` and `updated_at`, typed columns, and a concern prefix.

```mermaid
erDiagram
  organization_identity {
    text id PK "UUIDv7: the organization ID (from Better Auth)"
    text organization_statement "the signed stamp, stored exactly as received"
    integer created_at
    integer updated_at
  }
  organization_change_records {
    text id PK "UUIDv7"
    text request_id UK "the operation's own ID; a repeat finds this row"
    text kind "organizationProvisioned or workspaceCreated"
    text origin "person or signInProvisioning"
    text actor_person_id "from the verified person token; empty for signInProvisioning"
    text permission_checked "the permission the sign-in service confirmed; empty for signInProvisioning"
    text target_id "e.g. the workspace ID"
    integer created_at
    integer updated_at
  }
```

- `organization_identity` has **at most one row**, and it's written only by the internal provisioning request:
  - On a fresh store, every public command and read is refused until it's stamped, revealing nothing.
  - The organization never changes, and provisioning for a different organization fails. The signed statement can be replaced, but only by a valid statement for the same organization that names the stored statement's digest inside its signature. A setup retry without that never replaces anything: if a stamp is stored, it answers `Provisioned` and keeps it.
  - Central checks the stored statement against the sign-in service's published keys whenever it starts, and refuses every command if the check fails.
  - The Fleet object runs one transaction at a time (a Durable Object on Cloudflare; one writing connection on Tokio), so two first provisions can't both stamp it.
- **Your existing organization** keeps today's store. The deployment's config names its one organization ID, mapped to today's object `fleet` (Cloudflare) and `fleet.db` (Tokio), the same on both hosts. No other organization can take that name.
- **Two kinds of change record**, both in this one table:
  - *Set-up* (`origin: signInProvisioning`): written with the stamp. Its `request_id` is the organization ID, which is all the unchanged `ProvisionOrganization { organizationId }` request carries, so a retry finds the same record. It has no person and no permission; none is invented.
  - *A person's change* (`origin: person`): the verified person from the token, and the exact permission the sign-in service confirmed.
- Workspaces live in the reset's own `fleet_workspaces` table. B2 adds no workspace table.
- **Project ownership needs no new column or table.** A project belongs to O because O's Fleet directory (`fleet_project_directory`) lists it. An organization column on each project would only copy the stamp.
- No people are stored at central. Membership and roles stay in the sign-in service (Better Auth).
- **The SQL comes to you before B2 uses it**, like B1's.

b2-flows-text.text:
**Setting up an organization.** One idempotent transaction at central, so central needs no workflow of its own for it. The sign-in service makes a plain call (B1 builds no workflows). If the call fails or its reply is lost, the organization stays "setting up" until the call is made again, which nothing does automatically until the later workflow work. Any repeat is safe: it finds the same stamp and record and answers `Provisioned`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant SI as Sign-in service (plain call)
  participant L as The link
  participant F as Fleet object of organization O
  SI->>SI: sign the stamp statement for O (Better Auth signJWT, 120 days)
  SI->>L: ProvisionOrganization { organizationId: O, organizationStatement }
  L->>F: routed by Fleet { organization: O }
  F->>F: verify the statement against the published keys
  F->>F: one transaction: stamp organization_identity = O with the statement, write its change record
  F-->>SI: Provisioned
  Note over SI,F: a repeat finds the stamp already O and answers Provisioned, changing nothing
  SI->>SI: mark the organization ready (Better Auth fleetState)
```

**Renewing the stamp when the organization is used (your decisions of 9 Nov).** There's no daily job. Before sign-in sends anything to an organization's Fleet (a machine's token refresh, a machine-login approval, a forwarded admin command or lookup, a member or role revision push), it checks that organization's stamp record and renews the stamp if 60 days or less are left (your choice 3f). Browser sign-in, account pages and a person's own session refresh don't reach the Fleet, so they don't count.

The **stamp record** is extra columns on Better Auth's organization row (`additionalFields`, `input: false`, server-written, like `fleetState`):
- the confirmed stamp: its digest and expiry;
- the **sent** stamp: the full signed statement, while its answer is still unknown, and empty otherwise;
- the last renewal time;
- **unanswered** tries and **refused** tries, counted apart, with the last time and reason.

**Rules:**
1. **At most one stamp in doubt.** While a sent stamp is unanswered, sign-in only re-sends that same signed statement, byte-identical, and signs nothing new. If it landed, central's identical-replay path answers "already done". If it didn't, it still names the confirmed stamp, so central applies it.
2. **One writer per organization.** Setting, re-sending and clearing the sent stamp is a conditional row update: set only when empty, clear only when it still holds the same statement. Every sign-in instance and the key-change re-sign use the same guard.
3. **Answers.**
   - *Swapped* or *already done:* the sent stamp becomes the confirmed one, the sent column is cleared, and the renewal time is set.
   - *No answer or an unclear one:* one unanswered try, keep the sent stamp.
   - *Refused:* one refused try with its reason. If the refusal says the named stamp isn't the current one, sign-in reads central's current stamp, adopts it when its digest differs (even when it has expired, so a drifted and expired organization recovers: owner R29 change, 14 Nov), reconciles, and clears the sent column only once that's settled. An adopted expired stamp is due at once, so the next pass replaces it. Admin calls and revision pushes still require a valid stamp.
4. **The call itself.**
   - If the current stamp is still valid, the call goes ahead whatever renewal did.
   - If it has expired and renewal didn't land, the caller gets "try again shortly" (the existing unavailable answer). It is never treated as success.
5. **The limit.** A re-send works only while the sent stamp is valid, up to 120 days. If it expires still unanswered, sign-in can't recover on its own. The record keeps that condition for the admin page; notifications are later.
6. **Key change.** On a key change, every organization is re-signed before the old key is retired, including idle ones and ones with more than 60 days left. It then confirms each central holds the new key's statement and passes a cold restart. It goes through the same rules.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant SI as Sign-in service (before a Fleet call)
  participant F as Fleet object of O
  SI->>SI: record: 60 days or less left? a sent stamp still unanswered?
  SI->>SI: none sent: sign a new statement, replaces = confirmed digest; save it as sent (only if empty)
  SI->>F: ProvisionOrganization { O, sent statement } (re-sent byte-identical after a lost answer)
  F->>F: verify it; stored digest is the named one? then replace and write a change record
  F-->>SI: Provisioned / already done, or refused as stale
  SI->>SI: settle the record, then make the original call (or "try again shortly" if the stamp has expired)
```

**An admin command under the checked permission.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant You
  participant SI as Sign-in service
  participant F as Fleet object of your organization
  You->>SI: create workspace "research"
  SI->>SI: session current? your role holds workspace:create? (live check)
  SI->>F: CreateWorkspace + your person token + its confirmation naming workspace:create
  F->>F: guard: token valid, confirmation matches person, organization, permission and route; second factor fresh
  F->>F: one transaction: workspace in fleet_workspaces + change record
  F-->>You: Applied (or Refused: notPermitted · secondFactorRequired · conflict)
```

**What the guard checks** (carried over from the design's permission rules, unchanged):
- The person token is valid, its audience is central's admin address, and it's the right kind of token. Its expiry is rechecked at the applying transaction.
- The confirmation is bound to this token, person, session, organization, route permission and request, and it's used once.
- The applying transaction runs within **5 seconds of central receiving the request** (SD8), on central's own clock.
- Changes need a fresh second factor; reads are exempt.
- A refusal happens before anything about the subject is read, so it reveals nothing.

**Repeats and lost replies on `CreateWorkspace`.** Each request carries two identities:
- **The operation ID** (UUIDv7), chosen once by the sign-in admin page and kept on every retry. It goes through the Fleet object's existing request ledger, the reset's `fleet_request_decisions`, which keeps each request's canonical hash and its answer (`fleet_decision_step.rs`):
  - the same operation repeated gets its original answer, with the same workspace;
  - the same operation ID with a different body, person or organization is refused as a conflict;
  - two operations for the same canonical name (trimmed, then compared byte for byte) end with one workspace, and the second gets that workspace back.
- **A fresh confirmation** from the sign-in service's live check, for every attempt. A retry is checked again; an old confirmation is never reused.
- If the reply is lost after central commits, the retry finds the operation in the ledger and gets the original answer. The caller sees an honest "created" or "already created". The workspace and its record go through the Fleet's own write path and feed, not a separate insert.

**Every Fleet call carries its organization:** every resolver and call path, not just the two host address functions. Today's global Fleet call identities change to include it. A subject from another organization looks exactly like one that doesn't exist, before any project object is touched.

**A request for a project:** central checks that the token's organization equals the stamp, and that the project is in this Fleet's directory, before touching the project. A project that isn't listed is refused exactly like one that doesn't exist.

**A request naming the wrong organization:** the Fleet object compares the request's organization with its stamp. It refuses on a mismatch and changes nothing. A routing or forwarding bug therefore can't reach another organization's data.

**Simpler than before:** creating a workspace used to be "admitted", then applied later by another store. Now it's one transaction in one store, so its answer is `Applied` or `Refused`, and a lost reply is recovered through the operation ID. Project moves (B5) and remote starts (B8) keep their own existing result contracts, unchanged. The generic `Admitted` and `CommandStatus` shapes are no longer used by any B2 command; what happens to them is decided when B5 is designed.

**Decided 1 November (you, OD23), replacing that morning's "a central per organization":** two services. The sign-in service is the only one on the internet. Fleet central sits behind it, reached only over a link that only the sign-in service holds, and keeps each organization in its own storage. A new organization deploys nothing.

The organization authority, presence and session records are tables in that Fleet object. Nothing is stored per machine, and nothing spans organizations | only the sign-in service, over the link |

**The link.**
- **Cloudflare:** a service binding, `CENTRAL`, on the sign-in Worker. Central's Worker has no route and no custom domain, and `workers.dev` is off, so nothing on the internet resolves to it. The sign-in Worker forwards each Fleet request with `env.CENTRAL.fetch(request)`. Cloudflare's Workers pricing says a binding call adds no request fee; CPU time counts across both Workers.
- **Machine connections pass through it.** A local experiment on the pinned runtime (workerd 1.20261012.1, Miniflare 5.20261012.0-beta; `/tmp/2026-11-auth-front-central-spike/receipt.md`) carried a real WebSocket from a front Worker through a binding to a named Durable Object: the 101, messages both ways, unsolicited pushes, closes in both directions, and a forced hibernation and wake on the same socket. A direct request to the central Worker found nothing. Production idle timing, billing and long connections aren't measured.
- **Node and Tokio:** central listens only on a Unix socket in a directory owned by the deployment's user (mode 0700), never on a network address, and the Node sign-in host forwards to it. Both run on one machine; a native deployment split across machines isn't designed in this design.
- **Central's core takes no credential for the link.** Each host makes the link the only way in, so the core sees only requests that came over it.

**What the sign-in service sends, and what central still checks:**

| Request | The sign-in service | Central |
|---|---|---|
| A machine's connection (`public/v1/session`) and its renewals | forwards it unchanged, machine token included | checks the machine token itself (C9) against the sign-in service's published keys, then admits it at the organization authority the token names |
| A person's command or lookup, including provisioning a new organization's storage and the who-is-logged-in view (`public/admin`) | confirms the person's session is current (people sign-in R9), checks live that their role holds the permission the route needs (`hasPermission`), drops any confirmation the caller sent, attaches its own, created by its server for this one request and naming that permission; forwards it with the person token | checks the person token, then the permission guard: the attached confirmation's person, organization and permission match the request and the route, plus the second factor and freshness |
| `DecideDeviceLogin`, `DecideMachineToken`, `ProvisionOrganization` (`internal/`) | builds and sends them itself, on its own behalf; never forwards one from the internet | picks the operation from the route before parsing the body, then parses the body only as that operation's type ([service requests](#program-design--service-requests-r27-c7)) |

**How the objects sit on each host.** The same Rust core runs every object; each host only stores and schedules it. On Cloudflare each is a Durable Object. On Tokio each object is a slot in the one central process with its own SQLite file (today's `fleet` file and project files; the reset's D1 sets the layout). The Fleet object has **one durable-steps journal, one dispatcher and one alarm**, and every task kind, this design's included, registers on it on both hosts. What serializes the Fleet object's state is its storage transaction, not a queue: calls and frames may interleave between transactions, so every rule's guards and unknown-outcome handling hold at transaction boundaries. A rule that used to cross two of today's objects (for example the authority and the directory) is now **one transaction inside one Fleet object**. That is simpler, and it is reproved at B2 rather than carried over from the old proofs.

**Routing by organization, and the one check that guards it.** Central names the Fleet object from the organization in the request: `Fleet { organization }`, which this design adds at the reset's two address resolvers (Cloudflare `object_location.rs`, Tokio `native_objects.rs`); your organization keeps today's `fleet` object through a fixed mapping. A machine's connection is routed by the organization in its signed token. Each Fleet object is stamped with its organization when it's first created, and refuses, with nothing changed, any request whose organization differs (R55). So a forwarding or routing bug can't reach another organization's storage.

**Creating an organization** needs no deploy: an owner creates it in Better Auth through the sign-in service, which then sends `ProvisionOrganization` to that organization's Fleet object in one plain call; if it doesn't confirm, the organization stays "setting up" until the owner presses **Try again** (B2; nothing retries automatically until the later workflow work). The Fleet object exists from its first call (Cloudflare creates a named Durable Object on first access; Tokio creates its SQLite file), stamps itself with the organization, and records it in one transaction. See [admin commands](#program-design--admin-commands-and-lookups).

**Central asks the sign-in service nothing.** Its one outbound request is reading the sign-in service's published signing keys, cached, with one refetch on an unknown key ID. When the sign-in service learns an enrollment has ended (central's answer to `RevokeMachineEnrollment`, which names the ended enrollment and its client; the first `Grant` of a newer enrollment, which names the one it superseded; or central refusing a machine token for that enrollment), it disables that machine's client itself ([disabling a machine's client](#program-design--disabling-a-machine-s-client)).

**The scalars, exactly.** One accepted set each, written once as the JSON Schema `pattern` plus `x-maxUtf8Bytes` (F1's rule). The sign-in service's generated Zod enforces that pattern. The Rust constructor enforces the same accepted set with linear-time matching: the workspace's pinned `regex` crate, with any lookahead in the pattern written as an explicit check. No backtracking regex engine enters the runtime-free core, and no wider URL or email library decides acceptance. A three-way probe (Rust, the JSON Schema, JavaScript) proves the sets equal.
- **`HttpsUrl` and `ResourceUri`** (the sign-in address a Router is given; central's machine address, which machine tokens name) share one lexical rule. Their one constructor and schema live in `fleet-identity-protocol`, which both the Router and central core already depend on; neither copies the rule.
  - ASCII only, with no whitespace or control characters, and at most 2,048 bytes.
  - The scheme is `https`. `http` is allowed only when the host is `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`, for local test deployments.
  - The host is a lowercase DNS name in ASCII (an IDN as its `xn--` punycode, labels of 1–63 characters from `a–z 0–9 -`, never starting or ending with `-`), or one of those two loopback forms.
  - An optional port, 1–65535, written without leading zeros (so `:443` is valid and `:0443` is refused).
  - The path is empty, or starts with `/` followed by RFC 3986 path characters, percent-encoding included.
  - No user info, no query, no fragment.
  - Bytes are kept exactly as written and compared byte for byte, with no normalization.
- **`VerifiedEmail`** keeps the people sign-in design's existing rule: a provider-verified email, stored and compared lower-cased. Its syntax is the pinned Zod version's own `z.email()` pattern, copied verbatim as the schema `pattern`, ASCII only, at most 254 bytes. Whether an email was verified is provenance, not syntax: it comes from the provider sign-in or an accepted invitation, never from the string.
- `ReceiverId` and `PeerId` keep their existing owners and rules.
- Anything outside these sets is refused, and operators bear that limit.

**How a Router logs in and reaches central** (R41 unchanged):
- **The first login:** `fleet login --sign-in <address> --organization <id> --label <label>`. Later logins reuse the saved address. Nothing deployment-specific is in the repository.
- **The endpoints:** the Router reads the sign-in service's OAuth authorization-server metadata for its device and token endpoints. A small public document beside it, `/.well-known/fleet-login`, names the public Router device-login client. The document is closed: `{ "client_id": "<the public Router device-login client>" }`, and the Router refuses unknown fields. B3 serves it.
- **The resource** is central's machine address, one value in the sign-in service's configuration; a Router can't choose one.
- **The token answer** adds `fleet_central: { receiver, relay }`: central's authoritative receiver and relay peer IDs, from the sign-in service's configuration. They're public, and the connection needs them.
- **Where it's kept:** the Router saves the sign-in address, organization, enrollment, machine environment, receiver and relay in one row of a new `fleet_login` table in its existing fleet store (`fleet-cache.sqlite`, owned by `message-board-storage`'s `FleetCache`; no new database, owner 3 November; never the proxy's `state.sqlite`). The refresh credential stays in the encrypted store or in memory (R41). Until step 3 the Access reference stays configured, as today.
- **Connecting:** the Router connects at `<sign-in address>/fleet/v1/session`, which the sign-in service forwards to central's public namespace (below).
  - The sign-in address is the issuer identifier, which may carry a path (for example `https://host/api/auth`).
  - The `/fleet/` routes, and `/.well-known/fleet-login`, sit at that address's **origin**: `https://host/fleet/v1/session`. The issuer's path and any trailing slash never change them. Only the authorization-server metadata uses the issuer path, as RFC 8414 inserts it.
  - So `<sign-in address>/fleet/…` throughout this design means `<origin of the sign-in address>/fleet/…`.

**Two namespaces at central, and what the public edge may reach.** Every request arrives over the same link, so central can't tell from the link alone whether the sign-in service started a request or passed one on. The namespaces make that difference:
- **`public/`: what the sign-in service passes on from the internet,** and only this: `/fleet/v1/session` (a machine's connection, checked by its machine token) and `/fleet/admin/…` (a person's request, checked by the person token plus the sign-in service's own attached confirmation; any confirmation the caller sent is dropped). Every other path under `/fleet/` is refused at the sign-in service and never forwarded.
- **`internal/`: the decisions the sign-in service makes on its own behalf** (`DecideDeviceLogin`, `DecideMachineToken`, `ProvisionOrganization`). Only the sign-in core's central client builds these, from facts it has verified itself (a permission it checked, an organization Better Auth created); no public request is ever mapped here.
- **Adopting the saved route:** the Host's login owner lives for the Host's lifetime and watches the confirmed `fleet_login` row. When the receiver and relay first appear, or change, the Host rebuilds its collaboration runtime in-process (pump, writers, mail), using the existing lifecycle teardown and reassembly. Board admission stays closed until the rebuilt runtime has adopted them. Local MCP and API clients reconnect by their usual path, and an uncertain write stays uncertain, with no replay. A Host that starts with a saved row assembles with it directly. Nothing restarts the Host or Router process, and no routing ID is ever invented.
- **The Access reference until step 3** is the one already in `fleet/enrollment.json`. Only its Access part is read; the retired machine credential beside it never is. **One owner (agreed with the central storage reset, 3 November):** `fleet_login` is the only home of this Router's login and enrollment state, and `fleet/enrollment.json` is retired into it as a hard cutover, not kept beside it. `fleet/enrollment.json` changes in steps. **Until the switch (step 2)** today's login still uses it unchanged, machine credential included, and nothing touches it. **At step 2** the old login's code and its machine credential are removed, and the file shrinks to the Access reference (the Cloudflare client ID and secret key reference, or the self-hosted assertion key), which is transport configuration, not login state. **At step 3** the file is deleted with Access. `fleet_login` holds no Access column, and it has a row only after a confirmed device login. The reset's re-enrollment forget step clears only its named cache tables and never `fleet_login`. If the reset's D3 merges `fleet-cache.sqlite` and `fleet-outbox.sqlite` into one Router fleet store, `fleet_login` moves with it.
- This replaces F11's hand-written `login-config.json` and its login metadata file.

**What it costs, and who pays:**
- **The sign-in service is on every path.** When it's down, Fleet is unreachable too, machine connections included; they reconnect when it's back. Nothing in central's storage is lost.
- **Organizations share one deploy and one Worker's limits.** A bad central release reaches every organization; isolation is by storage, not deployment.
- **The link differs by host:** a service binding on Cloudflare, a Unix socket on Node and Tokio on one machine.
- **Gone, compared with that morning's design:** per-organization deploys and their runbook, the directory, the approval passed between Workers, the Router learning a per-organization central, the sign-in service's routing table, the service tokens between the two services, central's client key, and the credentials bound to an organization. The plan's removal list is on its own page.

program-design--admin-commands-and-looku.text:
> **Superseded placement (3 November).** Parts of this section were written for today's separate objects: a per-machine Connection object, a separate organization authority object, the Organization Registry and today's Registry. The central storage reset replaces them with **one Fleet object per organization plus one per project, and no new store** ([current map](#program-design--central-storage-with-the-fleet-structure-change)). Read this section's rules as rules: they still hold. Read its object names as homes in the current map:
> - the organization authority is a module with `machine_*`, `session_*` and `organization_*` tables in the Fleet object;
> - a Connection object's presence is the `machine_presence` table there;
> - the Registry's leases are the reset's Fleet tables;
> - the Organization Registry is withdrawn, and its "one machine, one organization" claim waits on your choice.
> A hand-off between two of those objects becomes one transaction in the Fleet object, reproved in B2–B4. **Don't build the objects named below.**

Every organization command and lookup names its organization and is refused unless the permission guard below passes. There is no fleet-wide role (OD24), and central keeps no roles at all: the sign-in service decides which person holds which permission ([people, roles and permissions](#program-design--people-roles-and-permissions)). Results are `Applied`, `Admitted { commandId }` (a published generic shape that no B2 command uses; `CreateWorkspace` is one transaction, answered `Applied`. Project moves and remote starts keep their own result contracts, below; the generic shape's fate is decided with B5), or `Refused { reason: NotPermitted | NotFound | Conflict | RecordUnwritable | SecondFactorRequired { within_seconds } }`; a refused command reveals nothing, and `SecondFactorRequired` (R53) is answered only to a caller whose confirmation names the route's permission, before anything else is checked or changed. **Audit (people sign-in R12):** every applied command writes its record (who, what changed, the organization, when) in the same transaction as the change, at the owner of the state it changes; if the record can't be written, that transaction fails and nothing changes. Each B2 command (`ProvisionOrganization`, `CreateWorkspace`) changes the organization's Fleet store and is recorded there, in the same transaction. Project-owned changes keep their own records in their project's store. `ProvisionOrganization` is recorded there too, as a system-initiated record with no person (B2). People changes are recorded in the sign-in service (OD26). An organization's audit view is assembled when read, by the admin surface, from each owner's records for that organization; nothing is copied, and an owner that can't be read is shown as unavailable.

**`CreateWorkspace` is one transaction** in the organization's Fleet object: the guard, the workspace in the reset's `fleet_workspaces`, and its change record, then `Applied`. No other store is involved, so it never answers `Admitted`. A repeat or a lost reply is settled through the Fleet's request ledger by the operation's ID: the same operation gets its original answer, and the same ID with a different body is a conflict (B2's doc). Project moves (B5) and remote starts (B8) keep their own result contracts; no B2 command uses the generic `Admitted`/`CommandStatus` shapes, whose fate is decided with B5. Creating a workspace is idempotent by its canonical name (the `ResourceName` value after its own trim, compared byte for byte).

**The list of organizations** is Better Auth's `organization` table in the sign-in service. Central has one Fleet object per provisioned organization, stamped with its ID by `ProvisionOrganization` in one idempotent transaction (B2's doc).

| Command | Request fields | What else it changes |
|---|---|---|
| `CreateWorkspace` | organizationId, name | — |
| `AllowMachine`, `WithdrawMachineAllowance` | organizationId, installation, workspaceId | — (its notice to the Switchboard comes with step 3) |
| `RevokeMachineEnrollment` (replaces the operator's `RevokeMachine`) | organizationId, installation | allowances withdrawn, sessions removed, the open connection closed; its answer, `Applied { ended: EndedMachineClient }`, names the client the sign-in service then disables ("Revoking a machine", below) |
| A device-code approval | not an admin command: the owner approves on the sign-in service's page, which sends `DecideDeviceLogin` (C7). The sign-in service vouches that the approver's session is current and that their role holds `machine:enroll`, checked live. The organization authority checks that vouching, within SD8, in the transaction that creates the enrollment, with its record. | — |
| `RemoveSession` | organizationId, session | — (its notice comes with step 3) |
| Lookups: `IdentityLookup`, `WorkspaceLookup` (its allowed machines), `MachineLookup`, `CommandStatus`, `WhoIsLoggedIn` (below) | organizationId plus the subject | — (shapes below, under "The four admin lookups"; `WhoIsLoggedIn`'s under "Who is logged in") |

**Permission guard (R13, OD25):** the caller presents a person access token whose audience is central's admin address, forwarded by the sign-in service with its confirmation attached. The sign-in service has confirmed, just before forwarding, that the person's session is current (the people sign-in design's privileged-decision confirmation, its R9, bound SD8) and, with `hasPermission`, that their role in the request's organization holds the permission the route needs. Its confirmation is created by its server for this one request and names the person, the session, the organization, the token it checked and that permission (`FleetPermission`). It drops any confirmation a caller sent. Central checks that the token's organization is the command's organization and the object's stamped organization; that the confirmation names this token's person, session and organization; that its permission is exactly the one the route requires (a table in the core, one row per route, never a role name); and that its request ID was never used before. SD8 is 5 seconds (the owner, 31 October). It is one setting, measured on central's injected clock from when central receives the forwarded request to when the owning transaction applies. It is never measured from the sign-in service's `checkedAt`, because the two clocks may differ by up to D. For a change the organization authority applies, the guard holds in that transaction: the confirmation must be within SD8 of it, and a confirmation is never reused for a later command. For a change another store applies, it holds when you ask (above). The guard refuses everyone else before any read or write.

**Who is logged in (R47–R50, C12).** A read-only lookup under the permission guard (`organization:view`). It changes nothing: it writes no record and starts no outbox step; presence reads change nothing at the Connection objects.

```rust
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct WhoIsLoggedIn { pub organization_id: OrganizationId }
#[serde(tag = "result", rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub enum WhoIsLoggedInResult {
    #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
    Snapshot { as_of: UnixMillis, machines: Vec<MachineRow> },
    Refused { reason: LookupRefusal },               // reveals nothing (R49); a lookup never answers secondFactorRequired
}                                                    // no answer at all, or an error, means unavailable
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct MachineRow {
    pub installation: InstallationId,
    pub label: MachineLabel,                         // from DecideDeviceLogin, kept on the enrollment
    pub enrollment: EnrollmentView,                  // { state: enrolled | revoked | expired, approvedBy: PersonId, approvedAt }
    pub may_serve: Vec<WorkspaceRef>,                // { workspaceId, name }: active allowances
    pub connection: ConnectionView,
    pub sessions: Vec<SessionRow>,                   // active only; removed and ended sessions are not listed
}
#[serde(tag = "state", rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub enum ConnectionView {
    #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
    Connected { since: UnixMillis, last_heard_at: UnixMillis },
    #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
    NotConnected { last_seen_at: Option<UnixMillis> }, // None: never connected on this enrollment
}
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct SessionRow {
    pub session: SessionRef,                         // its endpoint names the harness: Codex, Claude or Cursor
    pub project: ProjectRef,                         // { projectId, name }
    pub workspace: WorkspaceRef,
    pub isolation_kind: IsolationKind,
    pub started_at: UnixMillis,
    pub state: SessionStateView,                     // working | idle | unknown
}
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
```

- **One reading, one moment.** The organization authority reads its enrollments, allowances, sessions and activity in one transaction, at its own clock's `asOf`. In parallel it asks each enrolled machine's Connection object for its presence, with a deadline of half a refresh interval. It also asks its own Fleet object for the workspace and project names in the snapshot.
- **Never partial.** If the Fleet object or any Connection object can't answer in time, the whole lookup fails, and the page shows unavailable.
- **The derivations.**
  - A machine is `Connected` when its Connection object answers `Open`.
  - A revoked or expired enrollment always shows `NotConnected`, since its connection was closed and is refused.
  - A session's state is unknown unless its machine is connected and its latest activity report came on that same connection.
- **One organization.** Only machines with an enrollment in this organization are listed, which R34 already guarantees: one authority per organization.
- **Stage C's people rows never come from central.** The sign-in service's page builds them from Better Auth's own rows: each member's name, whether they are signed in now, and when they last signed in. Central holds no people. Bots join the lookup, as a new field, when bots exist.

**The four admin lookups (R14).** Read-only and under the permission guard (`organization:view`), like `WhoIsLoggedIn`: they write no record, start no outbox step, and never answer `secondFactorRequired`, because reads are exempt. Each answers only inside the organization it names. R14 asks for "a person's organizations", but an organization's owner may not learn of another organization (R34). The person lookup is answered by the sign-in service from Better Auth: that person's membership and role in this organization only (R14 says so). Central answers the session, workspace and machine lookups. A subject that doesn't exist and a subject in another organization both answer the same `unknown {}`, so nothing is revealed. Home: `identity_contract.rs`, beside the K12 shapes, whose `WorkspaceRef`, `ProjectRef` and `MachineLabel` they reuse.

```rust
#[serde(tag = "subject", rename_all = "camelCase", rename_all_fields = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub enum IdentityLookup {
    Session { organization_id: OrganizationId, session: SessionRef },
}
#[serde(tag = "result", rename_all = "camelCase", rename_all_fields = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub enum IdentityLookupResult {
    Session {
        session: SessionRef,
        machine: InstallationId,
        project: ProjectRef,
        workspace: WorkspaceRef,
        isolation: AgentIsolation,                    // E13, as registered
        machine_environment: MachineEnvironment,
        launch_context: LaunchContext,
        started_by: StartedBy,
        started_at: UnixMillis,
    },
    Unknown {},                                       // no such subject here, or it belongs to another organization
    Refused { reason: LookupRefusal },
}

#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct WorkspaceLookup { pub organization_id: OrganizationId, pub workspace_id: WorkspaceId }
#[serde(tag = "result", rename_all = "camelCase", rename_all_fields = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub enum WorkspaceLookupResult {
    Workspace { workspace: WorkspaceRef, allowed_machines: Vec<AllowedMachineRow> }, // active allowances only
    Unknown {},
    Refused { reason: LookupRefusal },
}
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct AllowedMachineRow { pub installation: InstallationId, pub label: MachineLabel }

#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct MachineLookup { pub organization_id: OrganizationId, pub installation: InstallationId }
#[serde(tag = "result", rename_all = "camelCase", rename_all_fields = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub enum MachineLookupResult {
    Machine {
        installation: InstallationId,
        organization_id: OrganizationId,              // always the one asked about (R34)
        label: MachineLabel,
        enrollment: MachineEnrollment,                // its latest: state, what authorized it, its machine client
        approved_at: UnixMillis,                      // when that enrollment's device code was approved: the same recorded fact as K12's EnrollmentView.approvedAt (C4)
        allowed_workspaces: Vec<WorkspaceRef>,        // active allowances
        shared_bucket: Vec<WorkspaceRef>,             // E14: workspaces that have had a Host-isolated session on it; shown, never enforced
    },
    Unknown {},
    Refused { reason: LookupRefusal },
}

#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct CommandStatus { pub organization_id: OrganizationId, pub command_id: CommandId } // CommandId: UUIDv7, from Admitted { commandId }
#[serde(tag = "result", rename_all = "camelCase", rename_all_fields = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub enum CommandStatusResult {
    Pending {},                                       // admitted; the other store hasn't applied it yet (it retries until it does)
    Applied {},
    Unknown {},
    Refused { reason: LookupRefusal },
}
```

**Creating and handing over organizations:** there is no fleet-wide role (you, 1 November, OD24). You create your first organization after your first sign-in, through Better Auth's own create, and become its owner. It's then provisioned at central, where B2 maps it onto today's Fleet storage. After that, **only you** may create another organization (A5, 3 November): `allowUserToCreateOrganization` answers yes only for the user the deployment's config names. Invites, an allowlist or Better Auth's admin plugin can widen it later without rework. The sign-in service then sends `ProvisionOrganization` on its own behalf. Handing over is adding another owner in Better Auth, then leaving. Today's Access-based operator caller (`AccessCaller::Owner`, `access_contract.rs:31–36`) is deleted with the other Access branches at step 2; Access identity proves nothing from then on. Open sign-up, where anyone signed in may create an organization and own it, waits with the people sign-in design's SD2.

**Central's routes:** until step 2, today's routes stay behind the Access gate, as now. From step 2 central has no public address at all (R55): every route is reached through the sign-in service's link. `public/v1/session` admits machines only by the machine token check; `public/admin` only by the person token plus the sign-in service's own attached confirmation; the `internal/` decision routes by their route, because only the sign-in core builds requests to them and the public edge never forwards there. Access stays in front of Fleet traffic until step 3, at the sign-in service's `/fleet/` path instead of central's hostname; removing it, and the request limit that replaces its edge protection, come with step 3.

**Central's outbound requests:** only reading the sign-in service's published signing keys, cached, with one refetch on an unknown key ID. There is no service caller and no client key.

program-design--people-roles-and-permiss.text:
**Three deciders, one job each (U47).** The sign-in service decides what people may do, on the sign-in path only. Fleet central decides what agents, bots and machines may do, from its own records, on every request they make; it never needs a person's role for that. The Switchboard decides tool calls in its own store. A WebSocket frame always acts as the machine and its sessions, never as a person, and no admin action is carried on a machine's connection.

**Better Auth's organization plugin holds people** (E19), configured in `sign-in-core` `src/organizations/`, following Better Auth's own way:

- **Roles from code, on the plugin's own resources.** `createAccessControl` declares the plugin's native statements (`defaultStatements`: `organization: [update, delete]`, `member: [create, update, delete]`, `invitation: [create, cancel]`) merged with the Fleet resources (E27). The plugin checks its own operations against those native names (inviting needs `invitation:create`, removing a member `member:delete`), and configured roles replace its default roles for those checks. So `ac.newRole` declares `owner` with `ownerAc`'s native statements plus every Fleet action, and `member` with nothing. Dynamic access control is off. The plugin's built-in `admin` role is not configured. `beforeAddMember`, `beforeUpdateMemberRole` and `beforeCreateInvitation` refuse any role but `owner` and `member`, and `beforeCreateInvitation` also refuses inviting as `owner` in this design.
- **Invitations** are on. Inviting needs the native `invitation:create`, so only owners can do it now. A person joins by accepting at their sign-in, with a provider-verified email that matches the invitation.
- **One owner per organization in this design, and it can't be removed.** The plugin's own last-owner check reads the owner count before a separate write, so two owners demoting or removing themselves at once could leave none, and D1 runs with transactions off. This design closes that by never letting the owner count go down: `beforeRemoveMember` refuses any target whose role is `owner`; the role-change and leave routes are not exposed; invitations are only as `member`. The organization's owner is its creator. Handing over (adding an owner, then leaving) comes later, with a guarded change that keeps at least one owner.
- **Which plugin routes reach the internet.** The sign-in service's public route list (`isPublicSignInRoute`) already refuses every route it doesn't name, raw organization routes included, before Better Auth dispatches. This design adds exactly the plugin's create-organization, invite-member, cancel-invitation, accept-invitation, remove-member and set-active routes. Not added: leave, update-member-role, delete-organization, and the list and get routes (the pages read Better Auth's rows on the server).
- **Creating an organization:** `allowUserToCreateOrganization` returns true only for the deployment's config-named owner (A5). There is no deploy-time initializer and no request-time seed: you sign in, then create your first organization through Better Auth's own create, and its creator-becomes-owner rule makes you its owner. Teams are off; they are not workspaces.
- **Which organization a request is for, and the person token's organization (K6):** the person token names one organization, taken at mint from the session's `activeOrganizationId` after a fresh read confirms the person is a member there; with no active organization, or one they no longer belong to, no person token is minted and the page asks them to choose (the plugin's set-active route). A `databaseHooks.session.create.before` hook sets `activeOrganizationId` when the person belongs to exactly one organization, as Better Auth documents, so your first sign-in and the owner CLI's first authorization get your one organization with no extra step. Every forwarded request names its organization, which must equal the token's; the sign-in service checks the permission in exactly that organization, with a fresh member read, so the active organization only scopes the token and never decides a permission.

**The permission each forwarded route needs.** The sign-in service checks it live: a fresh read of the `member` row for the verified token's person in the request's organization, then Better Auth's exported `hasPermission({ role, options, permissions, organizationId })` from `better-auth/plugins/organization`, with the configured roles and `useMemoryCache` off. The plugin's endpoint form (`auth.api.hasPermission`) needs a browser-cookie session, which a forwarded bearer request doesn't have, so every check, the device-code hooks included, uses the exported helper the same way. The helper's public type requires a real endpoint context, so every caller runs inside a Better Auth endpoint: the device-code hooks pass theirs, and the forwarding of `/fleet/admin/…` routes is a small plugin of our own whose endpoints (`createAuthEndpoint`, one per admin route) verify the person token, run the check with their own context and forward the request. The machine connection (`/fleet/v1/session`) needs no person check and stays in the request handler. It names the checked permission in the confirmation it attaches (K5):

| Route (admin command or lookup) | Permission |
|---|---|
| `CreateWorkspace` | `workspace:create` |
| `AllowMachine`, `WithdrawMachineAllowance` | `workspaceAdmin:allowMachine`, `workspaceAdmin:withdrawMachine` |
| `RemoveSession` | `workspaceAdmin:removeSession` |
| approving or denying a device code (`DecideDeviceLogin`) | `machine:enroll` |
| `RevokeMachineEnrollment` | `machine:revoke` |
| the lookups and `WhoIsLoggedIn` | `organization:view` |
| reading change records | `organization:readAudit` |
| the CLI's project commands (B5) | `project:read`, `project:repair`, `project:migrate`, `project:move`, `project:takeover`, `project:retire`, mapped per command in the overall design |

Inviting and removing people (the native `invitation:create`, `invitation:cancel`, `member:delete`) happen in Better Auth itself and never reach central; changing a role isn't offered in this design.

**Central's permission guard.** Central keeps no roles. For each `public/admin` request it checks, before any read or write: the person token's signature; that the attached confirmation was made for this request (its request ID, never reused), names the token's person and the request's organization, which is also the organization the object is stamped with (R55), and names exactly the permission the route needs; and that it is within SD8 and carries R53's second factor. Then the command's own checks run against central's records, in the same transaction as the change and its record. A confirmation for one permission never authorizes another route.

**A role change needs no push.** Central never holds roles, so demoting or removing someone takes effect at their next request, at the sign-in service's live check. The only gap is a change landing between that check and central applying the command, and SD8 bounds it. Machines a removed person approved keep working: a machine renews on its own enrollment (`DecideMachineToken`), and the owner revokes it with `machine:revoke` if it should go.

**Provisioning a new organization.** `fleetState` is an organization additional field with `defaultValue: 'settingUp'` and `input: false`, so the plugin's own insert stores `settingUp` and no caller can choose a value. `afterCreateOrganization` then sends `ProvisionOrganization { organizationId }` to central; on `Provisioned`, the sign-in service's own server code sets `ready`. If central doesn't confirm, the organization stays `settingUp`: forwarded requests for it are refused with `settingUp` (they never send `ProvisionOrganization` as a side effect), and the owner page shows "setting up" with **Try again**, an owner action that passes the session confirmation and live permission check before it repeats the idempotent call. A failure is reported, never hidden.

**People changes and their records (OD26, decided 2 November: record first, then confirm).** Better Auth on D1 runs with transactions off, so the plugin's own changes can't share one transaction with a record. Each people change has its own native hook pair in 1.7.11: inviting (`beforeCreateInvitation` / `afterCreateInvitation`), cancelling an invitation (`beforeCancelInvitation` / `afterCancelInvitation`), accepting (`beforeAcceptInvitation` / `afterAcceptInvitation`: the accept path inserts the member directly and never calls the `AddMember` hooks) and removing (`beforeRemoveMember` / `afterRemoveMember`). The `before*` hook writes the intent row to `sign_in_audit`, with its organization, and throws if it can't, so the change never happens without one; the `after*` hook writes the outcome row. **Re-sending an invitation is refused.** The invite route's `resend: true` extends a pending invitation's expiry and returns before `beforeCreateInvitation` runs, so it would change an invitation with no record; the sign-in service refuses a request carrying it before Better Auth sees it, and the plugin's cancel-on-re-invite option stays off. To re-invite, cancel, then invite again. **The actor is always the signed-in person who made the request,** taken from that request's authenticated session, never from the hook's payload: the remove hooks' `user` is the person being removed, not the one removing them. A record never confirmed stays unconfirmed, and is marked applied only by evidence covering that exact operation's completion, never from whether the person is a member now. An invitation row reading accepted proves only that step: the plugin marks the invitation accepted before it inserts the member, so in this design nothing proves a member addition completed, and such a record stays unconfirmed.
